status.en: 8 armed incidents reported in the past seven days, 53% fewer than the week before, most of them in Caracas, Valencia and Llano Alto.
status.nb: 8 væpnede hendelser meldt de siste sju dagene, 53 prosent færre enn uken før, flest i Caracas, Valencia og Llano Alto.

summary.en: The United States has lifted sanctions on Jorge Rodríguez, the president of Venezuela’s National Assembly, easing pressure on the opposition leadership. A major oil deal that could have supplied power to Venezuela has been halted, reducing the country’s energy prospects. Cuba’s electricity grid is collapsing, worsening regional energy strain that affects Venezuela. Families of two Trinidadians are demanding accountability from the United States for actions linked to the crisis. 2 battle-related deaths were recorded in 2007, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: USA har opphevet sanksjonene mot Jorge Rodríguez, presidenten i Venezuelas nasjonalforsamling, og lettet presset på opposisjonsledelsen. En stor oljetransaksjon som kunne ha levert kraft til Venezuela er stoppet, noe som reduserer landets energiperspektiver. Cubas strømnett kollapser, og forverrer den regionale energikrisen som påvirker Venezuela. Familien til to trinidadere krever ansvar fra USA for handlinger knyttet til krisen. To dødsfall i kamp ble registrert i 2007, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro and Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
